title: Tonkin`s first computer dictionary
summary: A satirical glossary of computing terms, circulated as a plain text file among bulletin board users and originally reprinted from a 1987 magazine article. Its entries define familiar jargon with sardonic, cynical wit: programmers are optimists who trust their code, users are realists who know better, and the operator is a beginner paid partly in soft drinks. Terms such as bug, glitch, kludge, benchmark, documentation, license and warranty are reframed as corporate double-talk or hard-won observations about failure. Many entries mock hardware and marketing, including the megabyte, the mouse, icons, user-friendly interfaces, word processors and the Pascal and C languages. The text also includes jokes about number systems such as binary, octal and hexadecimal, and a few bulletin board menu listings and cookie-style quotations. It is a humorous reference work rather than a serious dictionary, aimed at anyone who has spent time with personal computers in the 1980s and their frustrations.
